# Maximum-Entropy Learning {#sec-max-entropy}

::: {.callout-note title="Scope and status of this chapter"}
This chapter is an early scaffold, and it is worth being noted about what it
will eventually hold. *Maximum-entropy learning* is where the energy-based
viewpoint of @sec-energy-models meets the maximum-entropy principle of
@sec-entropy: among all models consistent with what we know, prefer the
maximally noncommittal one, which is the Gibbs distribution
$p(x) \propto e^{-E(x)}$, and then *learn* its energy. Read that broadly and
it is a large tent. A complete treatment should span at least:

- **Classical maximum-entropy models** — the Jaynes programme of @sec-entropy
  [@jaynes1957information], exponential families, and Gibbs distributions as
  the least-committal fit to moment constraints.
- **Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning** — policies of the form
  $\pi(a \mid s) \propto e^{Q(s,a)/\tau}$ that maximize reward *plus* entropy,
  from maximum-entropy inverse RL [@ziebart2008maxent] to energy-based
  policies and soft actor-critic [@haarnoja2017energy; @haarnoja2018sac].
- **Energy-based guidance and refinement** — the currently active,
  inference-time face of the same idea, where a (possibly composed) energy
  steers or polishes a generative process. This book gives it its own home in
  @sec-energy-reasoning; it belongs to the maximum-entropy family because
  guidance is descent on an energy and refinement is annealed sampling from a
  Gibbs distribution (@sec-free-energy).
- **Energy-based cooperative games** — our own line of work, recasting
  valuation through a maximum-entropy lens. This is the one strand written out
  below, as a worked example; it will be expanded in a later revision.

The sections that follow develop only the last of these. The others are
placeholders naming the intended territory, so that a reader knows what is
missing and where the neighbouring chapters already cover part of it.
:::

## A worked example: energy-based cooperative games {#sec-max-coop-games}

As one concrete instance of the programme above, consider a **valuation
problem** in machine learning: how much does a feature, data point, or player
contribute to an outcome? The classical answer is the **Shapley value** from
cooperative game theory, but it is one particular choice among many.

In *Energy-Based Learning for Cooperative Games* [@bian2022energybased], the
valuation problem is recast through an energy / maximum-entropy lens. A
cooperative game with characteristic function $v(S)$ over coalitions
$S \subseteq N$ induces a Gibbs distribution over coalitions,

$$
p(S) \propto \exp\big(v(S) / \tau\big),
$$

where $\tau$ is a temperature in exactly the sense of @sec-free-energy: as
$\tau \to 0$ the distribution concentrates on the highest-value coalitions,
while as $\tau \to \infty$ it flattens towards uniform. Applying the
maximum-entropy principle to game-theoretic valuations yields a **new class of
valuation methods**, of which the Shapley value arises as a special case.

## Why this is useful

- **Principled interpretation.** Valuations become the expectation of a
  well-defined quantity under a maximum-entropy distribution, giving a
  principled framework for interpreting AI models.
- **A family, not a point.** The temperature $\tau$ traces a spectrum of
  valuation schemes, enabling trade-offs beyond the single Shapley solution.
- **Bridges to physics.** The same Gibbs machinery is the one that carried the
  Ising energy into neural networks in the first place, by way of the Hopfield
  network [@hopfield1982] and the Boltzmann machine [@ackley1985];
  see @sec-free-energy.

## Takeaway

Maximizing entropy turns "which valuation should I use?" into "which constraints
do I believe?" — a shift that clarifies assumptions and unifies existing methods
under one roof.
